# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of the Varga & Holm comment on the Halden pilot

Sections 1–5 are strong and add real information beyond the earlier critiques, including mine:

- **The attrition finding is new and serious.** The Halden paper said all nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase." The microdata show seven of them happened after the reduced schedule had started. When I reviewed the Halden paper, I took its account of withdrawal at face value and treated it as harmless. This changes that.
- **Table 1 is the first direct evidence of manager bias.** In 19 of 23 organisations the manager's index exceeded the records-based index. A sign test on that split gives p ≈ 0.003, so the gap is very unlikely to be chance.
- **The actual-hours data turn a suspected problem into a measured one.**

Most of the arithmetic checks out:
- Hours: 34.6/40.3 = 0.859 and 34.8/40.4 = 0.861.
- Table 2 rows: 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%, 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%.
- Real revenue: 1.014/1.041 = −2.6%.

The comment's problems are that its headline conclusion goes well beyond its evidence, and that a few internal details don't hold.

## 1. The abstract misdescribes the analysis

**"Correcting the first three, the gain falls to 10.8%."** The first three problems are attrition, output measurement, and hours. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is not corrected anywhere. The 10.8% is still an estimate among survivors, as Section 6 itself says ("in the subset of survivors").

**"Four problems … account for most of the reported gain."** Revenue is the fourth problem, and it plays no part in the 23.4% per-hour figure. It is a legitimate separate criticism, but it does not "account for" any of the gain.

**The attrition bias could be bounded but isn't.** The microdata apparently include the withdrawn organisations, with monthly indices for the seven who left after month one or two. That allows an intention-to-treat estimate, or worst-case bounds that assign the dropouts low output. Without one of these, Section 1 shows the direction of the bias but says nothing about its size.

## 2. Table 2 changes the sample between rows

The rows use different subsets: 61, then 23, then 27, then 17 organisations. The drop from one row to the next mixes two things: the effect of each correction, and the effect of switching to a different group of organisations. To isolate each correction, all four specifications should be run on the same 17 organisations, which is possible since those 17 have both records and time tracking.

The Data Note rightly says the subsets weren't chosen at random. The comment should also show how they differ from the other organisations, especially by sector. Organisations that keep detailed time tracking and billing records are probably concentrated in professional services and IT.

## 3. The record-based output index has its own bias

The comment treats the records as the true measure of output and the manager index as biased. One of the listed record types is **"billable hours delivered."** In professional services, billable hours fall almost automatically when total hours fall. Using them as output therefore biases the records-based index *downward*, and "output per hour" becomes a measure of billable utilisation. Counts like tickets closed and units produced also ignore quality and complexity, which a manager's judgement might partly capture.

The finding that managers rated higher in 19 of 23 cases still stands. But the 3.8-point gap is the difference between two imperfect measures. It should not be read as the size of managers' overstatement. The comment should report the gap separately for organisations whose records are billable hours.

## 4. The hours breakdown doesn't add up

Section 3 attributes the smaller cut in hours to two sources:
- +0.7 hours per day on the four working days, which is +2.8 hours a week;
- 1.6 hours a week logged on the scheduled day off.

That is 4.4 extra hours on a 32-hour schedule, giving about 36.4 hours a week. The table reports 34.6. Measured against the baseline day of 8.06 hours (40.3 ÷ 5), the components give about 36.6. A total of 34.6 would mean roughly +0.25 hours per day, not +0.7. Either the per-day figure or the weekly average is wrong. This needs fixing, because the weekly average feeds directly into the 10.8%.

## 5. The novelty argument is the weakest part of the comment

**The extrapolation is miscalculated.** Energy fell 0.32 SD between month 3 and month 6, about 0.107 SD per month. At that rate the remaining 0.29 SD runs out about 2.7 months after month 6, at roughly **month 9**, not month 10. More importantly, drawing a straight line through two points can't establish a trend.

**Energy is not output.** The novelty claim concerns productivity. The pilot collected a **monthly** output index, and the comment has the microdata. The direct test is whether output per hour falls from month 1 to month 6, and the comment doesn't run it. It would still rest on the manager-reported index, but within-organisation trends are less affected by a constant rating bias.

**Novelty can cut both ways.** Early disruption followed by learning would make gains *grow* over time. The data do not support assuming the decline.

**"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter."** This sentence is rhetoric, and it doesn't justify the conclusion's much stronger claim that the gains are an artifact. "Not shown to be durable" is not the same as "shown to be an artifact."

## 6. "Entirely an artifact" goes beyond the evidence

The conclusion says reduced-hours per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty." Four things work against that:

1. **The comment's own residual.** About 11% remains after corrections. Attrition is unquantified and novelty is argued rather than measured, so the comment has shown that the true gain is smaller, not that it is zero.
2. **The Data Note.** It says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The conclusion then generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" in general.
3. **Selective use of Varden.** The comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature." It doesn't mention Varden's case-processing result: a randomised comparison, record-based output, timesheet hours, and +12.5% (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4) per actual hour at nine months. That is the design the comment itself recommends, apart from the follow-up length. A Hawthorne effect is also less able to explain it, because the control offices knew a trial was under way. The Varden figure has its own issues, notably paid overtime and the possibility of soaking up spare capacity. But the comment has to deal with it, and doesn't.
4. **Generalising from one pilot.** Even a fully successful demolition of Halden would say nothing about every reduced-hours scheme.

A conclusion the evidence supports would say roughly this: Halden overstated the per-hour gain by at least half. Its attrition was misreported. What remains is uncertain and untested for durability. Where output depends on staff presence, reduced hours reduce output.

## 7. The meetings section misdescribes the Varden analysis

- **"A subgroup … selected for analysis after the results were known."** The seven offices are *all* the treated offices in the case-processing stratum, and that stratum was defined before randomisation. Nothing was picked out of a larger set.
- **No credit for the hedging.** The Varden authors flagged the analysis as unregistered, warned that seven offices can't establish a mechanism, and registered a confirmatory test. The comment acknowledges none of this.
- **The real flaw is missed.** Varden collected meeting data only in month 6. Without a baseline, "offices that cut meetings most" can't be measured. Also, r = 0.71 with n = 7 has a 95% CI of roughly −0.1 to 0.95. These points are stronger than the cherry-picking charge.

"Should not be cited as a mechanism" is fair. The reasoning given for it is not.

## 8. Smaller points

- **Withdrawal reasons:** six organisations gave workload and two gave scheduling, which accounts for 8 of 9. What did the ninth give?
- **Retail figure:** the −11.2% for retail and hospitality rests on three organisations. Say so where the number appears.
- **Deflator:** CPI is a rough deflator for the revenue of business-services firms. A sector producer price index would be better, though the direction of the correction is clearly right.
- **Output per employee:** the most policy-relevant corrected figure isn't stated. Record-based output of about 95 means roughly a 5% fall in output per employee at full pay. That is what an employer would actually face.

## Bottom line

Sections 1–4 should stand. The attrition finding in particular calls for a response or correction from the Halden authors. The comment needs four changes:
1. Fix the abstract's description of what was corrected, and drop revenue from "accounts for the gain."
2. Run all of Table 2 on the same 17 organisations and bound the attrition bias using the withdrawn organisations' data.
3. Test novelty using the monthly output series, not energy scores, and correct the month-10 figure.
4. Replace "entirely an artifact" with a conclusion that matches the residual estimate and engages with Varden's case-processing result. Section 7 also needs rewriting.

I can draft a revised abstract and conclusion, or a same-sample version of Table 2's layout, if useful.
